quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Last census before Patrick's death in 1908; the 1890 census is largely lost, so 1900 is the final lifetime census. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

This browse of the page holding the household (imageArk ark:/61903/3:1:SYN9-IMG1 per log_002) decides between those readings by examining the ink directly. The 1880 household of Henry Mayfield (a_011 to a_014) indexes his wife as Atilla, and a son Isaac aged 6. This is the earlier reading of the wife's given name, with the census relationship line tying her to Henry. Browsing the original 1880 page confirms whether the enumerator wrote Atilla, or a spelling closer to Ottilie or Tillie, and confirms that this household is the same Henry and Isaac who appear in 1900. The next census after 1900. A woman widowed in 1900 and living with her son Isaac (who would be about 36) may be listed under a given name that matches or departs from the 1900 reading. Search by surname Mayfield in Goochland, with the candidate spellings from item 2, and by household member Isaac Mayfield. The 1910 entry's relationship and marital-status fields test whether the 1900 widow is the same woman, which is needed before her 1900 name is treated as hers.

The marriage of this woman to Henry Mayfield, which is the source of the given name she used when first married. Her marriage record may give a different name from the 1900 census, and the 1900 entry shows she was widowed, so the marriage is not the only one to check. Marriage records in Goochland for the 1870s-1890s are not a named collection in the locality entry (loc_001), and a catalog check did not return one, so this item is a browse of the county's marriage register images. The rationale does not assume that any marriage was her first, so the earlier marriages must also be checked.

Henry Mayfield, the 1880 head of household, is recorded as widowed in 1900 (a_007 is the woman's status). Search Henry Mayfield's death in Goochland with no given-name filter beyond Henry, and record any wife named in the entry.

Search by surname Mayfield in Goochland with each candidate given name spelling from item 2, and by the age and birthplace of about 1852 Virginia. The collection runs to 2026, so the item is sized to the collection rather than cut at the 1952 window end.

items.question: Besides Mary, John, Rebecca, William and Joseph, who were the other children of Thomas Hale (b. about 1810, Pennsylvania; d. 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and his wife Sarah?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

planItems.rationale: Survey of the tree before planning: Thomas Hale (born about 1810, Pennsylvania; died 1868, Greene County, Ohio) and Sarah Hale (no facts recorded). Five children are recorded, all born in Greene County: Mary (about 1836), John (about 1838), Rebecca (about 1841), William (about 1844), Joseph (about 1847). No source is attached to any of these facts. The 1850 census is name-searchable and names every household member with age, so it is the first full household listing and the place to test for any child under about 14 in 1850, including one born after Joseph. Search Thomas and Sarah Hale in Greene County and read the whole household.

The 1860 census is name-searchable and lists every household member with age and birthplace. It tests for children born 1848-1860 who were still at home, and for the five recorded children who were still in the household in 1860. Children who had left home by 1860 appear only if the parents are still listed, so read all members of the household.

Christening and birth entries for the children of Thomas and Sarah Hale, searched by the parents' names, not only the five known children. Ohio, Births and Christenings, 1821-1962 is name-searchable, and Ohio, Church Records, 1762-2008 is name-searchable and may hold Greene County church registers for the years before civil birth registration. A christening entry that names both parents can show a child the tree does not yet have. The window runs from the earliest plausible birth to 1850.

The marriage of Thomas Hale and Sarah, from Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2016, which is name-searchable. Thomas was born about 1810, so the marriage cannot be earlier than about 1828. Its date bounds the earliest possible birth of a child of this couple, and an earlier child would fall between the marriage and Mary's birth (about 1836). The marriage entry gives Sarah's maiden name and may name a bondsman, often a bride's father or brother, which is a FAN lead to her family. This item covers Greene County only. A marriage in another county or in Pennsylvania needs a locality survey before it is planned.

The 1840 census is name-searchable but names only the head of household. Other members appear only as tallies in age brackets. This tests whether the household held more children than the five named, through the number of children in each bracket. It does not name them, so it does not settle the question alone. The 1830 census is not planned because it also names only the head and would add less than this item.

The 1870 census is name-searchable. Thomas died in 1868, so Sarah may head a household with unmarried children still at home. The census lists members by dwelling, with ages and birthplaces; it does not record relationship to the head, which begins in 1880. Read every member of any household that includes Sarah, since a child missing from 1850 and 1860 may appear here.

The 1880 census is name-searchable and records each member's relationship to the head. If Sarah is a widow in 1880, the relationship field shows whether any named person is her child, which settles some doubtful members from 1870. Check the household for children and for grandchildren who may point to a child not yet in the tree.

The death of Thomas Hale in 1868, Greene County, from Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997 and Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001, both name-searchable. The entry may name surviving children or an informant, and a burial entry may list family members in the same plot. Search Thomas Hale with no surname filter on his given name, since the entry may use a variant spelling.

The estate of Thomas Hale. Ohio, Probate Records, 1789-1996 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Greene County probate file, not a name search. Locality survey: Greene County probate was held by the Court of Common Pleas until 1852 and by the Greene County Probate Court after, so the 1868 file is in the Probate Court's records. An estate file names heirs and widow, and any guardianship of minor children, so it can list children the census missed. The end date allows for guardianship filings after the estate closed.

A remarriage of Sarah Hale after Thomas died, from Ohio, Marriages, 1800-1958, which is name-searchable. A later marriage entry names her as a widow and can name her children or her previous husband. Search Sarah Hale and any maiden name found in the 1850 entry. A remarriage elsewhere is outside this item's jurisdiction.

The death of Sarah Hale, from Ohio, County Death Records, 1840-2001, which is name-searchable, and Ohio, Deaths and Burials, 1854-1997. Her death entry may name her children and parents as survivors or informants. The end date allows for Sarah surviving Thomas by many years; the tree has no death fact for her.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Mortality schedule. The 1850-1880 Mortality Schedules (name-searchable) list deaths in the year before each census. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

# Locality Guide: Feliciana Parish / East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana (1810-1835)

Feliciana Parish split into East and West Feliciana Parish in 1824. This is a geographic split: which successor parish holds a given record depends on where within the old parish the event occurred, and that is frequently unknown. Records for a family resident in the old parish before 1824 may be found under either successor's name after that date — search both.

planItems.jurisdiction: East Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
planItems.rationale: Silas Bankston (tree I1) was born about 1800 in Feliciana Parish and was recorded there in the 1820 census (tree fact F2, source S1). The parish split in 1824 geographically, so a marriage about 1828 could be entered in either successor. The East Feliciana marriage register (1824-1900) is name-searchable and is the first place to look for the marriage record, which should name the bride and the parish of the ceremony.

planItems.jurisdiction: West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
planItems.rationale: Same question as the East Feliciana item: the family's exact residence inside the old, undivided Feliciana Parish is not yet pinned down, so the marriage could be recorded in West Feliciana. The West Feliciana marriage register (1824-1900) is name-searchable and must be searched alongside the East register, not after it.

planItems.jurisdiction: East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
planItems.rationale: The East and West Feliciana marriage registers from 1824 are full-text searchable. A full-text search on the surname Bankston, run across both registers, catches entries where the name is misspelled or mis-indexed in the name index, which item 1 and item 2 can miss. This tests the same registers by a second route rather than a new repository.

If the parish registers in items 1-3 yield no entry for Silas, the statewide Louisiana marriage collection (1816-1906) is name-searchable and may hold a marriage record filed under a different parish or transcribed into a state-level register. It is the fallback for the East Feliciana item.

The Louisiana parish marriage collection (1787-1958) is name-searchable and covers the parish-level marriage registers across the state. It is the fallback for the West Feliciana item if that register does not return the marriage, and a check for a marriage recorded in a neighbouring parish near the family's residence.

The 1820 census in the tree (S1) places the Bankston household in Feliciana Parish, but the entry does not give a location within the parish. Neighbours in the enumeration (FAN) are the test: the families listed next to the Bankstons, and any Bankston household nearby, may fix the residence that decides East or West Feliciana. Neighbours and kin also appear as marriage bondsmen and witnesses, so their names feed items 1-3.

planItems.jurisdiction: East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States (Feliciana Parish before 1824)
planItems.rationale: The Louisiana wills and deeds collection (1700-2017) is name-searchable. Deeds of sale or purchase for Silas or his father in the old parish may state a boundary or a neighbour that locates the residence within the old parish, which decides which successor parish holds the marriage. A marriage contract or consent by a bride's father could also name the bride. The deed item is planned because it supplies the residence that item 1 and item 2 depend on.

planItems.jurisdiction: East and West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, United States
planItems.rationale: The 1830 census is name-searchable. It is the first census after the presumed 1828 marriage. It names only the head of household; the wife appears as an age bracket and no marriage place. The item finds whether Silas heads a household in either successor parish with a woman of marriage-age, which narrows the parish and gives a residence for item 1 and item 2 to use. It cannot name the spouse by itself.

Naturalization and declaration papers filed in Schuylkill County name a man's country of origin, port and date of arrival, and occupation, and they can establish whether Michael arrived in the US after 1870 or moved to the coal region from another US county. Births and christenings of children of Michael Sheahan in the Schuylkill parishes, after 1882, name the father's occupation, residence, and often his place of origin in the sacramental register. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

# Utah research guide (Weber County)

## Online records
- **U.S. federal censuses, 1940 and 1950** - indexed on FamilySearch; list each household member with relationship to the head.
- **Utah land and property records** - county recorder deeds; index online for some counties. Name grantors and grantees only.

1950 U.S. Census, Ogden, Weber County, Utah — household of John O and Olive H Applegarth with Alan. Corroborates the 1940 household.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Search Patrick Flynn with a birth range of about 1843-1847 in Schuylkill County, then read the whole household for Thomas Flynn (about 52, born Ireland) and for the household members the 1850 and 1860 records list. Patrick is about 55 and Thomas Flynn would be about 82 if alive, so this census tests whether the father is still in the household. Search Patrick Flynn born about 1843-1847 in Schuylkill County, and separately Thomas Flynn born about 1815-1822, and read the relationship column for each. quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

S2 (1860 U.S. Federal Census) is cited in the tree but no log entry or assertion covers it. The 1850 census (log_001) places Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household at dwelling 84, Schuylkill County, but only as inferred co-residence (a_004, supporting ps_001). The 1860 census (United States, Census, 1860, name-searchable) should show the same household with Patrick about 15 and any other children, which tests the co-residence. Search Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill with the household members; compare each age against the 1850 entry.

Follow Thomas Flynn (I2, b. ~1818, Ireland) and the household after 1860. The 1880 census (name-searchable, United States, Census, 1880) is the first to state each member's relationship to the head, so it can turn the inferred relationship in a_004 into a stated one for Patrick if he is still in the household. The 1870 census (name-searchable, United States, Census, 1870) gives the household between the two. Search the household members and, if Thomas has died, note the widow's household and any Flynn children listed with her; her household may name her as mother.

Follow Patrick Flynn (I1, d. 1908 Schuylkill County per F2) into his own household after he left his father's. The 1880 census records relationship to the head, so a widowed mother of Irish birth living with Patrick would be direct evidence she is his mother. The 1900 census (name-searchable, United States, Census, 1900) also lists his household and a possible mother. The 1890 census is not used because its surviving records are minimal (the count is 7,393 persons, 6,285 records).

F2 gives Patrick's death as 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, citing S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates), but no log entry or assertion has been extracted from it. A 1908 death falls under statewide certificates (from 1906). The certificate names the parents and the informant, which can state the father's name directly. Search Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 (name-searchable) for Patrick Flynn, then obtain the certificate image to read the parents' names and informant. This is the subject's own death entry (Step 3).

Fallback for the death certificate item. If the certificate is not found or does not name the parents, the burial register and cemetery record for Patrick Flynn (d. 1908) can confirm the burial place and the date, and can name a parent or a family plot. Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 (name-searchable) is the first place to look; the Catholic parish burial register is held by the parish, not the county.

Sibling baptisms as direct parentage evidence. A baptism of a sibling of Patrick that names Thomas Flynn as father would show the same parents, and it may give the mother's name, which the 1850 census does not. Pennsylvania Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (name-searchable) is the first search, keyed on Thomas Flynn as father. The Catholic register is held at the parish or the Archdiocese of Philadelphia (Schuylkill stayed with Philadelphia until 1961), and Patrick's own baptism may be in Ireland, where the tree records his birth, so a PA baptism is not assumed. The item covers children of the household after 1840.

Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother, dated before Patrick's birth (~1845). The marriage record confirms the couple as a unit and, if it was her first marriage, supplies her maiden name. The tree does not name the mother, and the 1850 census gives no wife name. Search Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991, and Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976 (both name-searchable), keyed on Thomas Flynn with any bride. If a marriage was in Ireland, the Pennsylvania search will not show it; the rationale does not assume a PA marriage. Also check for a second marriage of the widow later, since a surname on one record may be a prior married name.

A probate of Thomas Flynn's estate could name Patrick as a son and heir, which would be direct evidence of parentage. Thomas (b. ~1818, F3) was alive at the 1850 census, so his death is placed after 1850; the upper bound is Patrick's death in 1908 (F2), and a probate that names an heir before 1908 cannot be later than the subject's life. Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only in the collection, so this is an image browse of the Schuylkill County Register of Wills dockets (wills and administrations from 1811). Browse the index of Flynn administrations and wills for the years in the range.

Fallback for the probate item. The Schuylkill County Orphans' Court holds estate dockets and distributions from 1885 onward (a locality record type with access unknown). If Thomas Flynn's estate was settled in the orphans' court after 1885, the distribution list can name each heir, including Patrick. Confirm access with the court before relying on it.

FAN item. The 1850 census entry for Thomas Flynn's household (dwelling 84, Schuylkill County) is already logged (log_001). The dwellings next to it, read by image, may hold Irish-born Flynns or other households from the same origin place who could be kin, sponsors or lodgers. Their relationship to the household is not in the 1850 census, so a neighbor is only a lead; the item's purpose is to test whether a household shares the same Irish origin and surname as Thomas Flynn's. Browse the dwellings before and after 84 by image.

Thomas Flynn's death year is unknown, so a mortality schedule for 1850-1880 (United States Census (Mortality Schedule), 1850-1880, name-searchable) can show a death in the year before a census, with age and birthplace. A match with Thomas's age (about 32 at 1850) and Irish birthplace would give a date for the probate item, and a death entry can name a widow or children. The result is a lead, not proof of identity, and the entry must be checked against the household.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

Search Mikkel with the 1779 birth year and read the father's name from the entry; the subject's second element, Blyeberg, reads as a farm or residence name (Denmark Naming Customs: farm names record residence), so do not key on it. Entries run to about age 34 and rolls were renewed every three years, so 1789-1814 covers the boyhood enrolments and the later rolls.

Stagstrup church books (kirkebog) for 1763-1814 are browse-only: the volume is 3% name-searchable, so browse the baptism section by year to the entry for Mikkel, born 20 Aug 1779, baptised shortly after. A Danish baptism entry names both parents, which gives the father's given name (Niels, per the patronymic) and the mother. The register starts before 1779, so the baptism should exist.

It confirms the couple as a unit, and if the father's wife was a first marriage it gives the mother's maiden name, which census and death records often omit. The marriage date only corroborates a father named by other evidence; it does not by itself make Mikkel their child. Record each marriage of the woman found, since a remarriage would change which surname is hers.

Denmark Census, 1787-1930 is name-searchable. The 1787 census, when Mikkel was about 7, should place him in a household headed by his father. items.guide_markdown:
## Lincolnshire, England - 1750-1800

FamilySearch's 'England, Births and Christenings' collection (1473014) is a partial Legacy index: it does not index all records for this place or period, and no records or corrections are being added — a nil there is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists; search the parish register itself before concluding absence. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England,_Births_and_Christenings_-_FamilySearch_Historical_Records)

planItems.rationale: Mary Dawson's tree entry records only a birth of about 1772 in Lincolnshire, England (F1), with no parents, no source and no christening. A christening names the father and often the mother, which is the most direct route to the parents. Search the name-searchable FamilySearch collection 'England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975' (1473014). The locality guide flags that this collection is a partial Legacy index with no additions, so a nil here does not prove no christening exists. Item pli_002 covers the register itself.

Fallback for pli_001. The locality guide says a nil in collection 1473014 is a statement about the index, not proof that no christening exists, so the parish register itself must be searched before concluding absence. The parish is not yet identified (no place_search could resolve Lincolnshire), so search the register for Mary Dawson across the county's parishes, with birth-year spread 1762-1778 to cover the 'about 1772' estimate.

A marriage of Mary Dawson, roughly ages 17-33, usually names her father, and the banns or licence may record her parish of residence and a bondsman or surety, a FAN lead (BCG Standard 14). The marriage is not in the localities entry's collection set, and the collections search for Lincolnshire returned no rows, so this must be sought in the parish marriage register directly. Use the surname Dawson with no given-name filter, because the given name may be spelled variantly.

The subject's burial may state an age, a home parish or a birthplace, which matters because the parish baptism may not survive or may not be found. Plan it as a last-known-alive check for Mary Dawson, with no death date yet in the tree. Search without a surname-variant filter.

FAN search (required for a parentage question). Baptisms of siblings of Mary Dawson, and the godparents named in them, name the same parents and can reveal the family unit where the subject's own christening is missing. Search Dawson baptisms in the parishes found by pli_001 and pli_002 once a parish is known, and also the godparents named in them. Date window covers births of possible siblings of a child born about 1772.

Marriage of the candidate parents, which supplies the mother's maiden name (a census and a death record often omit it) and corroborates the father's date, but it does not by itself prove Mary is their child. No candidate couple exists yet, so this item depends on the father's name from pli_001 or pli_002 or pli_003. Dependency item: run it only after a candidate couple is named. If the mother had an earlier marriage, add a second search for her earlier marriage record.

quirks: Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org)
The typical Spanish name has four parts: two given names, the father's surname and the mother's surname. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Naming_Customs)

The subject's name would appear as Maria Guadalupe, often used as Lupe. Tree has no parent or relationship data, so nothing here is assumed.

A civil birth record for the subject, from Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration (1857-2000), is name-searchable for this place. It names both parents and may give the mother's maiden name, which the baptism may omit. Apply the paternal-surname quirk (Hernandez only). A dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other. Mexico, Marriages, 1570-1950 is name-searchable nationally, and Jalisco Catholic Church Records cover the same parish. The marriage confirms the couple as a unit, can supply the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage, and by date relative to the subject's birth (about 1895) corroborates a father named only indirectly. It does not by itself prove the subject is their child; that needs a baptism or birth record naming them (items 1 and 2).

Companion to item 3, testing whether the mother's surname is her birth name. If the mother married more than once, a marriage or civil record under an earlier surname would change which marriage record is the first. Search by the mother's given name without a surname, across the Jalisco civil marriage and Mexico Marriages collections, so that a prior married surname is not assumed. The result decides whether item 3 gives her maiden name.

Required FAN item. Siblings' baptisms, and baptisms where the couple served as godparents, name the same parents and often give the family's home parish. Search Mexico, Baptisms, 1560-1950 and Jalisco Catholic Church Records by the father's paternal surname with the mother's first surname kept as a second term, and do not key on the subject's name. A sibling record can confirm the parents even where the subject's own baptism is not indexed.

Fallback for items 1 and 2 if the subject is not found by name. Per the locality quirk, search through the parents instead: once a candidate parent is named by any record, search that parent's first surname with that parent's given name, leaving out the child's name. If indexed search fails, browse the baptism register images of Jalisco Catholic Church Records for the subject's probable birth window, parish by parish in Guadalajara.

Parents' death records, from Mexico, Deaths, 1680-1940 (name-searchable nationally), are a secondary test for parentage. A death record for a parent often names the spouse and children and gives the parent's age, and it can be checked against the candidate parents once found in items 1 to 3. Date range runs to 1940 because the parents may have died long after the subject's birth. This item does not establish parentage alone.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.
